title: Flood-displaced Nepalis brace for winter; Some still in tents - WORLD News Group
description: Flood-displaced Nepalis brace for winter; Some still in tents  WORLD News Group
publisher.title: WORLD News Group
full_article:
Many Nepalis living in northern regions affected by the devastating Aug. 26 flash floods need supplies to survive the winter. Some of those displaced are still living in tents months after the disaster, said Matthew Hanning, CEO of International Nepal Fellowship’s branch in the United Kingdom. Last week, he visited several villages and towns affected by the floods as part of his work with the nonprofit, which provides healthcare and education services along with disaster relief. As a non-governmental relief organization, INF is working to provide winter essentials—thick mattresses, blankets, gloves, and hats, Hanning told WORLD on Monday. The non-governmental relief organization has been in the country since the early 1950s, working on health and development initiatives, “serving with love because God first loved us,” according to its website.

The Aug. 26 floods wiped entire villages off the map near Nepal’s border with Tibet. At least 1,500 people perished, and 5,600 remain missing, according to the UN. The Nepali government has officially ended the rescue phase of its response and is now focusing on rebuilding roads, bridges, critical infrastructure, and homes, according to Hanning. But recovery will take years. Crews often have to dig out tons of dirt and debris deposited by the floods before they can begin rebuilding. Hanning said he saw several roads where bulldozers moved over six feet of sand just to get down to the original road surface.

Further complicating the rebuilding process, both locals and the Nepali government are often unsure whether to reconstruct homes in the same area, knowing that another flood could sweep through the steep valleys, Hanning said. He learned that many of the locals had moved to northern Nepal after losing their homes in a massive 2015 earthquake, then had to start over after the August floods. In one northern village he visited, Syepru Besi, roughly a third of homes had been severely damaged or destroyed, he said. At least one INF staff member has a missing relative, Hanning said.

Representatives of Christian churches in one of the affected areas told him they were still trying to process their grief. Some of their pastors and congregants were still missing, and four churches were destroyed in the floods, he said. But they are trying to care for their communities and show Christ’s love, despite the grief, he said. Nepali Christians are a tiny minority in their majority-Hindu and Buddhist country, and they typically worship on Saturday because Sunday is a workday. At the service Hanning attended on Saturday, the Nepali congregation sang a song with the words, “Father, you are king over the flood. I will be still and know that you are God,” he said.

Kathmandu. In October 2026, one lakh thirty-two thousand 814 foreign tourists entered Nepal. According to the information provided by the Nepal Tourism Board, more than four thousand foreign tourists entered Nepal this year compared to last year's October month.

According to the board, the highest number of 17 thousand 437 American tourists arrived. Last year, 13 thousand 286 American tourists came in the same month. This year, 12 thousand 97 Indian tourists came to visit Nepal in October, while last year's October had 17 thousand 298.

In October 2026, 11 thousand 695 tourists from China visited Nepal. British tourists arrived in fourth place.

full_article: Kathmandu. Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri will pay an official visit to Nepal on Wednesday, Kartik 18 and Thursday, Kartik 19. He is coming to Nepal at the friendly invitation of Foreign Ministry Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has stated that there will be a bilateral discussion between Foreign Secretary Rai and Indian Foreign Secretary Misri during the visit. During the discussion, both sides will review all aspects of Nepal-India relations and exchange views on various issues of mutual interest. It is believed that the discussion will further strengthen the close and friendly relations that have existed between the two countries for a long time. During his stay in Nepal, Foreign Secretary Misri will also pay courtesy calls on high-level dignitaries of Nepal. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has stated that Indian Foreign Secretary Misri is scheduled to depart from Kathmandu to New Delhi on Kartik 19 after completing his two-day official visit.

The charity curry night was organised by the Amesbury Community Bingo Group and led by Dr Monica Devendran, a Wiltshire councillor and founder of the group, following a call for support after severe flooding in the country.

The event brought together residents, businesses, volunteers, and members of the Nepalese community in a show of solidarity and generosity.

title: Nepal Premier League: Kathmandu Gurkhas and Sudurpaschim Royals Secure Victories - Ratopati
description: Nepal Premier League: Kathmandu Gurkhas and Sudurpaschim Royals Secure Victories  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Two matches were played in the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) on Monday. Teams chasing targets won both matches. In the first match, Kathmandu Gurkhas registered their first win in the tournament by defeating Karnali Yaks by 4 wickets, while in the second match, Sudurpaschim Royals defeated Chitwan Rhinos by 5 wickets.

The results of both matches on Monday not only affected the tournament's points table but also kept the teams' form and players' performance in discussion. For Kathmandu, captain Karan KC's aggressive batting became the basis for victory, while for Sudurpaschim, Brandon McMullen played a short but impressive innings.

On the other hand, the NPL journey of David Warner and Sikandar Raza, familiar faces in world cricket, also made Monday's match more interesting.

In the first match on Monday, Kathmandu Gurkhas were given a target of 181 runs to win. Kathmandu, which was defeated by 8 wickets in the first match of the tournament by Janakpur Bolts, needed to win this match. Therefore, the team was expected to adopt an aggressive strategy from the beginning.

Australian experienced batsman David Warner and Smith Patel took to the field as Kathmandu's openers. This was Warner's first match in the NPL. Warner, who has extensive experience in world cricket, was seen as an attraction of the tournament.

However, Warner could not play a big innings in his NPL debut. He scored 16 runs off 10 balls with 3 fours. Before being bowled by captain Sompal Kami, he had started aggressively. The other opener, Smith Patel, was also out for 9 runs off 11 balls. Warner's international cricket career, however, is very successful. He has played 112 Tests, 161 ODIs, and 110 T20 Internationals for Australia. Across all three formats, he has scored 18,995 runs. He was an important member of the Australian team that won the 2015 and 2023 ODI World Cups and the 2021 T20 World Cup. In the 2021 T20 World Cup, he was also named the Player of the Tournament.

Although Warner got out early, Kathmandu made an excellent comeback in the chase. Rashid Khan, who came in at number four, scored a half-century. He scored 50 runs off 32 balls with 3 fours and 2 sixes.

Captain Karan KC also showed his ability in batting. He scored 44 runs off 20 balls with 4 fours and 3 sixes. Karan's aggressive batting brought Kathmandu close to victory. Later, Jahandad Khan remained unbeaten on 22 with 2 sixes and 1 four off 10 balls, and Kathmandu completed the target in 19.4 overs, losing 6 wickets. Sompal Kami and Hussain Talat took 2 wickets each for Karnali. Mark Watt and Nandan Yadav took 1 wicket each but could not help the team win.

Earlier, Karnali, who chose to bat after losing the toss, scored 180 runs for 6 wickets in 20 overs. Ariful Islam scored 44 runs with 3 sixes and 5 fours off 22 balls. Hussain Talat scored 40 runs off 30 balls, while Pawan Sarraf remained unbeaten on 27 and Gulshan Jha scored 20 runs.

Captain Karan KC took 2 wickets for Kathmandu. Shahab Alam, Dev Shah, and Santosh Yadav took 1 wicket each. Thus, by completing the target of 181 runs, Kathmandu achieved its first victory in the tournament. The team, defeated in the first match, made a comeback in the second match and handed Karnali their first defeat of the tournament.

In the second match on Monday, Sudurpaschim Royals defeated Chitwan Rhinos by 5 wickets. This match was also an NPL debut for Chitwan captain Sikandar Raza. The experienced Zimbabwean all-rounder Raza tried to contribute with both bat and ball in his first NPL match. However, his debut was not memorable.

In batting, he could only score 15 runs off 20 balls with 1 four. In bowling, he spent 26 runs in 4 overs but could not take a wicket. However, due to his experience and all-round ability in world cricket, Chitwan expects a significant contribution from him in the upcoming matches.

Raza has been playing for the Zimbabwe national team since 2013. He has played 22 Tests, 162 ODIs, and 145 T20 Internationals for Zimbabwe. He has scored 4,824 runs in ODIs and 3,261 runs in T20 Internationals. In bowling, he has taken 101 wickets in ODIs and 116 wickets in T20 Internationals. He is known as a player who can make an impact with both bat and ball.

In Raza's debut match, Chitwan batted first and could only score 129 runs for 6 wickets in 20 overs. Ravi Bopara scored the highest 49 runs for Chitwan. He hit 2 sixes and 3 fours off 40 balls. Although he missed the half-century by one run, Bopara tried to stabilize the innings, but he did not get enough support from other batsmen.

David Malan scored 16, Arjun Saud 15, and Raza himself scored 15 runs. Vivek Yadav scored 17 runs. Scott Kuggeleijn of Sudurpaschim took 2 wickets. Captain Dipendra Singh Airee, Hemant Dhami, and Anil Kharel took 1 wicket each.

Sudurpaschim, chasing a modest target of 130, batted aggressively. Opener Brandon McMullen scored 43 runs off 21 balls with 6 fours and 2 sixes. His strike rate was above 204.

Dr. Ishan Pandey scored 25 runs off 29 balls. In the middle order, Arif Sheikh and Sherfane Rutherford also made necessary contributions, and Sudurpaschim completed the target in 16.4 overs, losing 5 wickets.

Chitwan's Ranjit Kumar took 3 wickets but could not prevent the team from losing; Rijan Dhakal took 1 wicket.

Rutherford Praises Nepali Cricket

West Indies cricketer Sherfane Rutherford, who contributed to Sudurpaschim's victory, said that the future of Nepali cricket is bright. Speaking at a press conference after the match, he praised the good talent among Nepali players.

Rutherford, who is returning home after playing four matches, said that his time in Nepal was very good. He said that he was impressed by the beauty of Nepal and the hospitality of the Nepali people on his first visit.

“I wondered what it would be like when I first came to Nepal. But after coming here, I called my family and told them that Nepal is very beautiful and the people here are very loving,” he said. He expressed confidence that more Nepali players will get opportunities in international cricket in the future, seeing the good potential in Nepali players. He said that the participation of international players in Nepal would also benefit Nepali cricket.

Rutherford also praised Sudurpaschim captain Dipendra Singh Airee extensively. He said he was impressed by Dipendra's playing style, leadership qualities, and behavior.

“Dipendra is an excellent player. Looking at the innings he played in the World Cup, Nepali players can learn a lot from him. He plays fearlessly and is very sensible. His energy on the field is good, and off the field, he is equally humble and friendly,” he said. Sharing his experience of playing with Dipendra in Canada before, Rutherford said that players like him should get more international opportunities.

He said that although the pitch was a bit difficult in the match against Chitwan, the team played with composure. He said that even though batting was not easy from the wicket in the second innings, the team's victory was possible because the players played according to the situation.

He took the results of two wins and two losses in the initial four matches as normal. He said that making mistakes at the beginning of the tournament and learning from them is also important. “There is no guarantee of victory in cricket all the time. But the right thinking and mindset are important. Our team is balanced and has the potential to win the title,” he said.

Rutherford also expressed his views on the issue of playing on a wet ground the previous day. He said that the ground was not suitable for playing from the perspective of player safety. “That ground was not fit to play from both player safety and cricket perspectives. I personally told the manager that I would not play. But I love my team and was ready to do anything for the team,” he said.

He said that even though the result of that match did not go in their favor, the team made a good comeback against Chitwan by forgetting it.

Speaking about the standard of the NPL, Rutherford said that every franchise league has its own characteristics. He believes that although the NPL is in its early stages, it will become bigger and better in the future.

“I don't want to compare the NPL with any league. Every league is special in its own way. The NPL is in its early stages. With time, it will become bigger and better,” he said.

He said that the participation of international players and the good performance of Nepali players will take the NPL to greater heights. He mentioned that the world is watching Nepali cricket now and said that there is great potential for cricket in Nepal.

Ranjit's Goal is to Take Chitwan to the Final

After the loss to Sudurpaschim, Chitwan Rhinos spinner Ranjit Kumar said that the goal is to win the remaining matches and take the team to the final.

Speaking to reporters after the match against Sudurpaschim at the TU Cricket Ground in Kirtipur on Monday, Ranjit said that one loss will not change the team's goal. He said that he would do his best to perform well in the upcoming matches, get wins, and take the team to the final.

“Our main goal now is to win the remaining matches. I will try my best to take the team to the final,” he said.

Chitwan has played three matches in the tournament so far. With one win, one loss, and one match being abandoned due to rain, Chitwan has accumulated three points. In such a situation, the results of the remaining matches will be important for the team.

Ranjit also said that the team's preparation is good. He said that even though there were some changes in the players and leadership, it did not affect the team's preparation. He said that although they did not get the opportunity to prepare abroad, the closed training held in Hetauda was effective.

“Our preparation has been very good. We had closed training in Hetauda. That camp was very fruitful for us,” he said.

Ranjit said that the team is also benefiting from the experience of Chitwan's head coach Sohail Tanvir. He said that Tanvir, who is also a former player, shares his international cricket experience with the players, which makes it easier to play on the field.

“He has a lot of international cricket experience. He is constantly sharing his experiences with us players. Because of that, it is very easy for us to play on the field,” Ranjit said.

Although Chitwan lost the match against Sudurpaschim, Ranjit performed well individually. He made a significant contribution to the team's bowling by getting three Sudurpaschim players out.

Although he could not convert his individual performance into a team victory, Ranjit said that his focus is now on the upcoming matches. Chitwan's goal will also be to strengthen their chances of reaching the final by winning the remaining matches.

The results of both matches on Monday have also affected the points table. Sudurpaschim, with four points from four matches, has moved up to third place. Chitwan has dropped one place to fifth.

Kathmandu has opened its account in the tournament with its first win. Karnali suffered its first defeat after four matches.

Overall, Monday's matches saw the presence of foreign players, the debut of new players, and decisive performances by Nepali players. The arrival of international-level players like Warner and Raza has increased the attraction of the NPL. However, the teams' wins and losses, rather than their individual performances, became the main story of Monday's matches.

Two more matches of the NPL are scheduled for Tuesday. In the first match, Biratnagar Kings and Janakpur Bolts will clash, while in the second match, Lumbini Lions and Pokhara Avengers will compete.

title: In first high-level visit after new government’s arrival, Foreign Secretary Misri to visit Nepal on November 4-5 - The Hindu
description: In first high-level visit after new government’s arrival, Foreign Secretary Misri to visit Nepal on November 4-5  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri will pay a two-day visit to Kathmandu on November 4 and 5, the Ministry of External Affairs announced on Monday (November 2, 2026). This will be the first visit by Mr. Misri to Nepal since Prime Minister Balendra Shah took charge in March this year following the election that was conducted under an interim government. A visit to India by Mr. Shah is understandably part of the agenda that will be discussed when Mr. Misri meets officials in Kathmandu.

“Foreign Secretary’s upcoming visit continues the tradition of regular high-level exchanges between the two countries and will help further enhance the comprehensive bilateral partnership,” said the Ministry in an announcement. The visit by Mr. Misri to Kathmandu will be keenly watched as it comes amid a slew of reforms that Nepal’s post-Gen-Z uprising government is in the process of rolling out.

A new phase in India-Nepal relations

Apart from Mr. Shah’s visit to India, Mr. Misri’s conversations in Kathmandu are likely to feature the appointment of a new Ambassador of Nepal to New Delhi. Nepali Embassy has been without an Ambassador for several months since the previous Ambassador, Shankar Prasad Sharma, returned home. Nepali diplomatic sources told The Hindu earlier that Kathmandu was waiting for the agrément (diplomatic approval) for new envoy Nischal Nath Pandey to take charge in the embassy here. India’s continued assistance to the disaster in Bhote Koshi river is also expected to be on the agenda.

Even as Mr. Misri's visit was being announced by the Ministry, a welfare association of former Indian Army soldiers took out a protest in Kathmandu on Monday (November 2) demanding that Gurkha recruitment into the Indian Army be resumed. Recruitment of Gurkha soldiers remains suspended since the Agnipath scheme was introduced by the Government of India.

The Hindu had earlier reported that Mr. Misri was expected to visit Nepal in May, but the visit was postponed ostensibly because Mr. Shah had prioritised domestic challenges. The India visit by Mr. Shah, if it materialises, will be the first bilateral visit abroad by the leader who came into prominence during the September 2025 Gen-Z uprising that overthrew the government of Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli. Mr. Misri had visited Kathmandu previously for two days in August 2025 and had met Mr. Oli.

In the past few months, India has hosted Nepal’s Foreign Minister Sisir Khanal, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, and Home Minister Sudan Gurung, who visited Delhi to participate in the first BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation) meet held on October 13, 2026. India has also hosted the head of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) Rabi Lamichhane in the first week of June when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Mr. Lamichhane paid a personal visit to India last week to pray at the pilgrimage centres in Kainchi Dham in Uttarakhand and the Kamakhya temple in Guwahati.

Mr. Lamichhane had described this visit as “personal and not political”. “There are no political meetings planned. Since this is a personal visit, I urge people not to read politics into it,” said Mr. Lamichhane before starting the visit.

title: Nepal must move beyond climate victimhood and take a leadership role: Experts - Khabarhub
description: Nepal must move beyond climate victimhood and take a leadership role: Experts  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal must move beyond highlighting its vulnerability to climate change and establish itself as a credible contributor to regional and global climate solutions through concrete domestic action, scientific evidence and stronger regional cooperation, speakers said at a national policy symposium held in Kathmandu on Monday.

The Institute for Strategic and Socio-Economic Research (ISSR) and Khabarhub organised the symposium under the theme “Nepal After UNGA: From Climate Victims to Climate Leadership”.

The discussions focused on how Nepal could translate its recent engagement at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) into measurable national achievements and stronger climate diplomacy ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31), scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye.

The symposium highlighted that Nepal’s geographical vulnerability, experience of climate-related disasters and longstanding commitment to multilateralism provide a strong foundation for climate leadership. However, participants stressed that international recognition must be supported by effective policies, institutional capacity, strategic investment and tangible results.

A key message emerging from the discussions was the need to advance the “Sagarmatha to the Sea” vision by recognising the interconnected relationship between Himalayan glaciers, river systems, downstream communities, coastal regions and the sea. The symposium emphasised that climate change in the Himalayas is not merely a national concern but has wider implications for water security, agriculture, energy, livelihoods and ecological stability across South Asia.

Participants called for stronger regional cooperation in climate science, glacier and river-basin monitoring, information sharing, early warning systems and disaster preparedness. In this regard, the proposed Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism was identified as a possible framework for strengthening regional collaboration.

The discussions also underscored the importance of placing climate-affected communities at the centre of national policies and international negotiations. Participants noted that the consequences of climate disasters extend beyond immediate loss of life and physical damage, affecting livelihoods, agriculture, education, health services, cultural heritage and local economies.

They called for systematic documentation of the experiences of disaster-affected families, farmers, women, Indigenous communities and other vulnerable groups to ensure that their concerns are reflected in climate assessments and policy decisions.

Nepal faced a series of devastating disasters in recent months, resulting in significant losses of lives and property. The August disaster in Bhotekoshi and the floods in the Kaligandaki River in September caused extensive damage. Heavy rainfall has also triggered floods and landslides, disrupting road networks and transportation in various parts of the country. Experts believe climate change could be a major contributing factor behind the increasing frequency and intensity of such disasters.

The issue has gained added significance ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31), scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. As world leaders prepare to gather to discuss climate action, policy priorities and future commitments, Nepali stakeholders have stressed the need for the country to strengthen its international climate diplomacy and emerge as a proactive voice for climate justice.

Speaking at the programme, former Nepal government Chief Secretary and Chairman of ISSR, Shankar Das Bairagi described climate change as a long-term and structural challenge rather than merely a technical issue. Referring to the approval of USD 20 million from the climate loss and damage fund, he said Nepal should view the development positively and make effective use of the available resources. He also argued that climate leadership could become an important source of Nepal’s soft power and strengthen its position in international affairs.

Shankar Das Bairagi

Likewise, presenting a working paper, former secretary and climate expert Dr. Pem Kandel highlighted the widening gap between the financial resources required to address climate change and the commitments made by the international community.

According to Kandel, approximately USD 7.5 trillion in annual investment will be required by 2030 to limit global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius. The required investment is projected to reach USD 8.8 trillion annually between 2031 and 2050. However, international financial commitments remain far below the estimated requirements, he noted.

Pem Kandel

Professor Dr. Sangita Singh of the Institute of Engineering Studies stressed that disaster resilience must begin with a proper understanding of geographical vulnerabilities. She argued that even well-constructed houses and infrastructure could remain vulnerable if they are built without adequately considering local geographical and geological conditions.

Sangita Singh

She also emphasized that resources received through the loss and damage fund should not be limited to rebuilding damaged houses and infrastructure. A portion should be invested in research, scientific studies and long-term planning to reduce future disaster risks.

Referring to the Bhotekoshi disaster, Singh said Nepal should treat the tragedy as an opportunity to strengthen disaster preparedness, develop climate-resilient policies and ensure environmentally responsible reconstruction. She further stressed that Nepal should not be defined solely by its vulnerability to climate change but should highlight its efforts to protect the environment and the fragile Himalayan ecosystem.

Similarly, Dr. Krishna Devkota, Vice-Chairperson of the Gandaki Province Policy and Planning Commission, said Nepal must strengthen its federal, provincial and local institutions to establish itself as a credible climate leader.

Dr. Krishna Devkota

He emphasized the importance of coordination among all three levels of government in addressing climate change and reducing disaster risks. He also said Gandaki Province had been prioritizing disaster risk reduction and measures to address the challenges arising from climate change.

Associate Professor Chandralal Pandey of Kathmandu University highlighted the need for meaningful youth participation in climate action and disaster management. He observed that youth representation in decision-making processes, from local community organizations to national policymaking institutions, often remained largely symbolic.

Chandralal Pandey

Pandey argued that young people must be directly involved in policy formulation, development planning and implementation rather than being included merely to fulfil formal representation requirements. He also stressed the need to expand access to climate education, disaster-related training and practical, employment-oriented learning opportunities to empower young people.

Researcher Dr. Sudan Kumar Oli pointed out that although several international and domestic financing mechanisms have been established to address climate change, the available resources remain inadequate compared to the scale of the challenge.

Sudan Kumar Oli

He also highlighted the complexities of post-disaster recovery and rehabilitation, stressing the need to improve resource mobilization and ensure that financial assistance reaches affected communities efficiently and without unnecessary delays.

The discussions underscored that Nepal’s transition from climate vulnerability to climate leadership will require more than international advocacy. Strong institutions, evidence-based policymaking, adequate financing, scientific research, climate-resilient infrastructure and meaningful public participation will be essential to turning its climate commitments into tangible action.

Speakers at the interaction also stressed the need to strengthen regional cooperation, arguing that Nepal cannot effectively confront climate-related disasters on its own. They called for internal institutional and structural reforms to advance climate diplomacy and enhance the country’s capacity to engage with regional and international partners.

Everest climber Jangbu Sherpa, comparing his experiences of climbing Everest in 2008 and 2018, said the amount of snow and ice in the Everest and Khumbu regions had noticeably declined. He warned that a disaster similar to the one in Bhotekoshi could cause massive loss of life and property if it struck the Khumbu region.

Jangbu Sherpa

Sherpa also said declining snow levels in the Himalayas were creating additional challenges for mountaineering. He cautioned that continued climate change could leave the Everest region without snow within the next 30 years.

Chheten Gyalpo, a resident of Syafrubesi in Rasuwa who was affected by the Bhotekoshi disaster, called on all three levels of government to prioritize climate change and disaster risk reduction.

Sharing his personal experience, Gyalpo said the Himalayas, which once filled him with pride and admiration, had increasingly become a source of fear because of the growing threat of climate-related disasters. He also stressed that potential disaster risks must be carefully assessed before undertaking development infrastructure projects.

Former Asian Development Bank Vice-President Dr. Bindunath Lohani emphasized the need to mobilize greater financial resources for climate change research and disaster management. He called for strengthening universities and research institutions to improve scientific understanding and policymaking.

Dr. Bindunath Lohani

Lohani also highlighted the importance of improving data collection and analysis, while stressing that infrastructure development must follow more climate-resilient and risk-informed approaches.

Environmentalist Purna Chandra Lal Rajbhandari called for greater attention to disaster preparedness and management, noting that Nepal continues to face recurring disasters every year.

Former Nepal government secretary Kewal Prasad Bhandari said Nepal’s participation in COP31 could carry greater weight if Prime Minister Balendra Shah attended the conference in person. He also cautioned that accessing the approved funding from the Climate Change Loss and Damage Fund could involve a lengthy process, requiring the government to prepare accordingly.

Kewal Prasad Bhandari

Bhandari stressed that Nepal should not delay its climate action while waiting for international financial assistance. Instead, the country must take proactive measures and mobilize available resources without making implementation dependent on the arrival of external funding.

Similarly, Bishnu Adhikari, Governance Director of The Asia Foundation, observed that international financial commitments alone would not guarantee effective climate action. He said Nepal must strengthen its domestic institutions and implementation mechanisms to ensure that international assistance is properly utilized.

Independent energy entrepreneur Suman Joshi said the Bhotekoshi disaster had resulted not only in the destruction of infrastructure but also in the loss of skilled human resources. She pointed out that Nepal’s neighbouring countries are among the major carbon emitters and argued that their contribution to climate-related impacts in Nepal should be recognized.

Joshi stressed that Nepal must urge neighbouring countries to assume greater responsibility for the consequences of climate change and strengthen regional accountability.

Niranjan Devkota, Research Fellow at the Policy Research Institute, called for more comprehensive preparations to address disaster risks and climate change. He emphasized the need for long-term planning rather than relying on short-term responses after disasters occur.

Likewise, Sushma Rai, Programme Coordinator at the Centre for Asian Futures of the Asian Institute of Diplomacy and International Affairs, argued that Nepal should place greater emphasis on disaster preparedness rather than focusing primarily on disaster response and management.

She stressed that regional cooperation was essential to reducing disaster risks and mitigating climate change impacts, calling for stronger collaboration among countries across the region.

Rai also emphasized the importance of involving local communities in climate-related discussions and incorporating indigenous knowledge into policymaking and disaster preparedness strategies.

Young environmentalist Sandhya Dhungana stressed that climate policies must go beyond formal commitments and ensure effective implementation. She also emphasized that funds received through international climate financing mechanisms should be mobilized at the local level to directly benefit vulnerable communities.

Sandhya Dhungana

More than 35 participants attended the programme, including environmentalists, former government officials, residents of Himalayan regions, academics, journalists, policymakers, hydropower entrepreneurs and representatives of various organizations.

Nepal spent an estimated Rs 10 lakh (INR) from its disaster management fund to rescue six Indian trekkers who had allegedly entered the restricted Upper Dolpa region without mandatory permits, ignored warnings against travelling during heavy snowfall and pressed ahead, leaving their guide behind.The group, comprising five trekkers from West Bengal and one from Andhra Pradesh, spent two nights stranded in the mountains before a helicopter evacuated them on Monday. Authorities subsequently charged them NPR 1.6 lakh (approximately Rs 98,000) in permit fees and penalties but reduced the fines considering their physical condition after the ordeal.The six trekkers — Moumita Halder, Piyali Koley, Jajla Trivedi Kumar, Aditya Singha, Diplina Biswas and Rajesh De — were rescued at dawn on Monday from Danigad, around 300km northwest of Kathmandu. The helicopter made three round trips, evacuating two trekkers on each round. All six were taken to Dunai, the Dolpa district headquarters, where they underwent medical examinations and were subsequently discharged. The operation required a civilian helicopter after a Nepal Army aircraft scheduled to arrive on Sunday developed a technical problem and could not fly.Dolpa chief district officer Junu Hamal toldthat authorities could have imposed a maximum fine of NPR 50,000 (Rs 31,250) on each trekker but instead charged NPR 20,000 (Rs 12,500) per person.The trekkers also paid $40 (Rs 3,800) each towards mandatory permits. "Seeing their condition, we gave them a concession," Hamal said. However, she criticised the group for ignoring repeated warnings from security personnel, local residents and their guide, putting both themselves and rescuers at risk."Such irresponsible behaviour is unacceptable," she said. "Nepal is already struggling to find funds for reconstruction after the devastating flash floods on Aug 26. At a time when we are trying to rebuild affected communities, having to spend precious disaster funds on a rescue necessitated by such carelessness and irresponsible behaviour is extremely frustrating," she said.The district administration had restricted travel to Upper Dolpa from Oct 29 because of heavy snowfall, but the trekkers allegedly left their guide behind and continued towards Shey-Phoksundo lake despite warnings. They became stranded near the Numa La and Baga La mountain passes, and their guide alerted authorities on Saturday evening. Snow and poor mobile connectivity complicated rescue efforts. title: Nepal deserves its own place on the global education map - The Koala News
description: Nepal deserves its own place on the global education map  The Koala News
publisher.title: The Koala News
full_article:
Post the sector gathering at AIEC, much of the conversation was about Australia: its policies, its settings, its competitiveness. It is worth asking how that conversation sounds from Nepal, which supplied about 9 per cent of Australia’s international students in the first half of 2026, making it the third-largest source country, according to Australian government data.

Picture a familiar moment in an education counselling office in Nepal. A student is excited about a university overseas. A parent wants to know something more immediate: can the family afford the entire degree, not just the first semester? Another student is weighing Australia against Japan or the UK, with questions about language, living costs and the prospects after graduation.

These are illustrative situations, not quotations from a particular meeting. But they reflect the questions I encounter in more than a decade of working with Australian education providers and education stakeholders across South Asia. They also explain why Nepal needs to be understood as more than an additional stop on a regional recruitment itinerary.

International institutions understandably plan across South Asia. India commands attention because of the scale and diversity of its market. Nepal is often considered alongside it, which is practical and natural given the countries’ close ties. Yet regional planning should leave room for country-specific understanding. Nepal has its own economic realities, education ecosystem and distinctive patterns of student mobility. Recognising that does not diminish any neighbour.

The numbers are only the beginning

Australia is not the only destination where Nepal’s weight is growing. In 2025, the UK granted 19,553 sponsored study visas to Nepali main applicants, a 60 per cent year-on-year rise, according to Home Office statistics. These measures describe different things—student numbers in Australia and visa grants in the UK—but both show Nepal’s importance.

Nepali students also consider Japan, the United States, Canada, South Korea, India and other destinations. Each offers different courses, costs, language environments and possibilities after graduation. It would be a mistake to interpret movement towards one destination as a simple rejection of another.

Overseas study is also not simply labour migration: students leave for particular qualifications, research and experiences, not for a single economic reason.

What families are really weighing

Consider the different priorities within one family. A student may be excited by a course, a city or a friend’s experience abroad. A parent may want to know whether part-time earnings are being assumed in the financial plan, what support is available if the student struggles, and whether the qualification has value beyond a visa outcome. Neither is asking the wrong question.

This is why the most useful counselling does more than compare countries. It helps families test whether a programme suits the student’s academic background, whether the total cost is manageable, and whether expectations about employment and future pathways are realistic. Nepal’s students are not one uniform group: school leavers, postgraduate applicants and working professionals make different calculations. Kathmandu matters, but it is not the whole market.

A market to understand, not just enter

When an overseas provider considers Nepal, the first questions are often about agents, popular courses and enrolment potential. I would encourage one more question before any recruitment target is set: which students would genuinely benefit from what this institution offers?

Nepal has a well-established education consultancy industry. Good advisers translate complex admission requirements into practical guidance and provide valuable local knowledge. Institutions should work with them as professional partners, with clear training, transparent information and attention to student outcomes—not simply application volume. Providers also need to understand Nepal’s evolving rules for consultancies and foreign-affiliated programmes, taking local advice before making commitments.

A few meetings in Kathmandu can introduce an institution to the market. They cannot substitute for listening to students, parents, schools, colleges, alumni and advisers across different communities. A country-specific strategy can sit comfortably within a wider South Asian plan; it simply starts with better questions.

The story continues after graduation

Outbound student statistics rarely tell us what happens next. Some Nepali graduates build careers and families overseas and maintain strong ties to home. Others return with new skills, professional contacts or business ideas. Many contribute across borders without fitting neatly into either category.

It is tempting to frame this entirely as brain drain or brain gain. Nepal needs a more useful conversation about how internationally acquired knowledge can circulate—through mentoring, entrepreneurship, research, investment and collaboration. We should also ask what would make returning more attractive: professional opportunities, institutional capacity and a credible environment in which to apply those skills.

There is another dimension. Nepal is not only sending students abroad; it is also developing opportunities for international education at home. Foreign-affiliated programmes and transnational education partnerships create possibilities for curriculum collaboration, faculty development and access to qualifications without requiring every student to leave. These arrangements need strong academic standards and appropriate oversight, but they deserve a place alongside outbound mobility in the international discussion.

Give Nepal its own conversation

None of this diminishes the importance of India or any other South Asian country. Regional relationships are valuable, and institutions will continue to plan across borders. The point is simpler: Nepal’s students, families, advisers, graduates and domestic institutions have their own story, and the scale of its international education connections makes that story internationally relevant.

For providers, this means understanding Nepal before recruiting from it. For policymakers, it means connecting mobility with skills and education at home. For journalists, it means reporting Nepal as more than a passing reference in a story about another country’s visa policy.

For Australia, this matters in practical ways. Every policy announcement made in Canberra is read in Nepali homes as a question about cost, certainty and trust. Providers that understand those questions, and answer them honestly, will be better placed than those that treat Nepal as an extension of a wider regional pipeline.

Nepal does not need to be compared with a larger neighbour to establish its importance. Its students have already made the case.

title: Expanding flower business in Nepal brings both opportunities and challenges to local growers - Floral Daily
description: Expanding flower business in Nepal brings both opportunities and challenges to local growers  Floral Daily
publisher.title: Floral Daily
full_article:
As Tihar approaches, farmers in Gundu, Bhaktapur, are busy picking flowers and weaving garlands. Going to the fields early in the morning to pick flowers and working together with family members in the afternoon to prepare garlands has become their daily routine. These very flowers decorate someone's home and enhance the joy of someone's festival. However, for the farmers who produce flowers and bring them to the market, this season is also a time to balance earnings with prices and markets.

Flower cultivation in Nepal is no longer limited to the desire to decorate one's courtyard. Connecting with commercial production, employment, trade, and export potential, it is expanding as a distinct business sector in agriculture. Spreading across 54 districts of the country, the floriculture business has started generating an annual turnover of more than Rs 3 billion. According to data from the Floriculture Association Nepal (FAN), more than 50,000 people have found direct and indirect employment in this sector.

According to FAN, commercial flower farming is taking place across approximately 250 hectares nationwide. More than 1,145 entrepreneurs are involved in this sector. Flower farming is expanding in districts including the Kathmandu Valley as well as Jhapa, Ilam, Dhankuta, Morang, Sunsari, Chitwan, Kavre, Kaski, Rupandehi, Banke, Dang, and Kailali.

In the fiscal year 2025/26, the annual turnover of the floriculture business reached Rs 3.27 billion. Compared to Rs 2.94 billion in the previous year, the turnover increased by about 12 percent in a single year.

title: India seeks Nepal reset: China’s footprint, border disputes to test bilateral relations - MillenniumPost
description: India seeks Nepal reset: China’s footprint, border disputes to test bilateral relations  MillenniumPost
publisher.title: MillenniumPost
full_article:
New Delhi: India’s diplomatic relations with Nepal are anticipated to see a renewed momentum following Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri’s two-day trip to Kathmandu this week - on Thursday and Friday - to discuss various bilateral issues. This visit comes as a key moment for India-Nepal relations following the political change in Kathmandu. Officials believe that this will offer New Delhi an opportunity to strengthen its relations with the new government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah.

India and Nepal have been witnessing strong friendly relations, even in the past, with significant progress made across various issues. As per the Ministry of External Affairs communique, Misri’s visit will continue the high-level regular exchange between the two nations to further strengthen all aspects of bilateral relations.

However, there are various strategic concerns to consider about this close relationship - l disputes over territory, increasing Chinese influence, open border security and differing economic and connectivity policies. How the two neighbouring nations approach these issues will be key to shaping their relations.

The most sensitive issue is the dispute over the territory of Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura. Nepal added this territory to its new political map in 2020; however, India does not recognise these territorial claims. This has been reignited following the objections raised by Nepal over using the Lipulekh route for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. As this is situated on the India-China border it has wider implications.

With growing economic and strategic influence from China, New Delhi must consider how this will affect its bilateral relations. Beijing has invested in infrastructure, Belt and Road Initiative projects and proposed railway lines to increase its influence in Nepal. Kathmandu are trying to spread its foreign partnerships to gain strategic independence; however, India wants to make sure it is not losing any ground from a security perspective. New Delhi will want to keep Nepal confident by working with them on development projects and keeping up the dialogue.

Security will also be a key issue. The open border between the two nations of roughly 1751km has brought them closer together socially, culturally and economically but has caused issues regarding human trafficking, drug smuggling and organised crime. The recent coordination meeting between the Sashastra Seema Bal and Armed Police Force demonstrates how important information sharing, collaboration and border control are to both nations.

Energy offers a lot of scope for the countries to work together. Nepal has great potential in hydro power and India’s electricity needs are growing. Projects such as the Arun-III (900MW), Lower Arun Hydropower and transmission lines show how important energy is becoming. Trade of electricity between Nepal, India and Bangladesh can help improve regional connectivity.

Water management will also be an important issue. Nepal and India share several rivers such as the Kosi, Gandak and Mahakali. Controlling flooding, maintaining embankments and irrigation can cause issues for both nations. Working together on managing the rivers is important, especially considering the flood-prone areas of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

Economically, India is still Nepal’s largest trading partner. Bilateral trade was around $9.38 billion in 2025-26. Railway links, integrated checkpoints, oil pipelines, road links and trade are important aspects. As Nepal are looking to diversify their trade routes, it will be important that India is a dependable and competitive partner.

Defence is another important aspect. Joint exercises such as Surya Kiran and military training are important. The two nations have had historic relationships between their armies. They will also need to address the long-standing request from Nepal for a review of the Treaty of Peace and Friendship signed in 1950.

This visit will give an opportunity to assess the many aspects that are involved in bilateral relations. While one visit cannot solve all of the long-standing differences, by keeping the dialogue up to date it will help to avoid issues becoming too contentious.

Overall, the challenge for India is to keep the close relationship they have with Nepal, whilst respecting their sovereignty and dealing with the increasing influence of China. For Nepal, they want to keep their strategic independence but also gain from their geographical, economic and historic relationship with India.

This diplomatic meeting will be watched closely to see if the two nations can move forward and create a more predictable strategic relationship.

title: Nepal arrests foreign Christians amid crackdown on missionary activities - Muslim Network TV
description: Nepal arrests foreign Christians amid crackdown on missionary activities  Muslim Network TV
publisher.title: Muslim Network TV
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (MNTV) — Nepali authorities have arrested 10 foreign nationals, most of them medical professionals, over suspected Christian missionary activities during a free medical camp, marking the second major detention of foreign Christians within a month and raising concerns about growing restrictions on religious activities in the Hindu-majority country.

The detainees, including five Americans, three Brazilians and two Canadians, were arrested on Oct. 28 in Morang district in eastern Nepal, where they had been organizing a four-day medical camp for local residents.

According to local authorities, the foreign nationals entered Nepal on tourist visas and were conducting medical activities without obtaining the necessary authorization.

The group, associated with an organization called Mercy Development, had arrived in Nepal in October and was reportedly operating the health camp in cooperation with a local Protestant church.

Police detained the volunteers following complaints from local residents and transferred them to the Department of Immigration in Kathmandu for further investigation. Their travel documents were also confiscated.

Dipesh Shrestha, deputy general secretary of the National Christian Federation Nepal, said local authorities had approved the medical camp, which operated from Oct. 25 to 28.

However, he acknowledged that organizers had not obtained mandatory authorization from the Nepal Medical Council, the country’s regulatory body for medical professionals.

The arrests follow a similar operation on Oct. 9, when Nepali authorities detained 24 South Korean Christians in the same district over religious activities conducted while visiting on tourist visas.

Immigration authorities subsequently canceled their visas, imposed fines of 50,000 Nepali rupees, approximately $328, on each individual and barred them from entering Nepal for three years.

The repeated detentions have prompted criticism from Christian organizations, which argue that authorities are increasingly treating humanitarian assistance and religious activities as grounds for punitive immigration action.

Bidur Adhikari, chairman of Media Action for Advocacy Nepal, an organization advocating for Christian minority rights, warned that portraying humanitarian medical assistance as religious conversion activities could deepen mistrust and social divisions.

“Framing humanitarian medical aid as evangelism or proselytization activities fosters fear, alienation and social division,” Adhikari said.

His organization condemned what it described as the criminalization of immigration violations and warned that repeated enforcement actions were creating anxiety among Nepal’s Christian population.

The advocacy group demanded the unconditional release of the detained foreigners and the return of their travel documents.

Nepal became a secular republic in 2008 after centuries of Hindu monarchy, formally recognizing religious freedom while maintaining legal restrictions on religious conversion.

Under Nepal’s criminal laws, proselytizing and activities intended to convert people from one religion to another can carry prison sentences of up to five years and substantial fines.

title: SIT Probes Forged Signatures, Suspects Girdhari Sahu Nepal Escape As Legal Feud Deepens - ETV Bharat

full_article:
Amid raids at several locations, there is a buzz that he might have fled to Nepal. Meanwhile, names of Satendra and Kalpana Mishra have emerged during the investigation. Both are said to be close associates of Sahu. The Special Investigation Team (SIT) is currently searching for them as well. While their specific roles are still unclear, they have now been brought within the scope of the investigation.

The case took a new turn on October 16, when Girdhari Lal Sahu released a video accusing his wife, cabinet Minister Rekha Arya, of possessing alleged illegal assets worth approximately ₹210 crore.

By making these allegations public, Sahu brought the matter to the fore, igniting a debate and demands for an investigation. Subsequently, on October 17, advocate Pankaj Singh Chhetri filed a written complaint with the Vigilance Establishment, calling for an impartial inquiry into the Minister’s alleged assets.

The complaint demanded an investigation into her movable and immovable properties, bank accounts, fixed deposits (FDs), investments, shares, business interests, and sources of income. The complainant also urged that an investigation be conducted under the provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act, and that a formal case be registered should sufficient grounds be established. Investigative agencies are unable to uncover any evidence to substantiate the allegations made by Girdhari Lal Sahu, who has he provided any proof to support his claims. Amidst this dispute, on October 15, Minister Rekha Arya filed a case against her husband, Girdhari Lal Sahu, at the Cantt Kotwali police station in Dehradun.

The First Information Report (FIR) contains serious allegations, including the concealment of a prior marriage, physical assault, mental harassment, the use of casteist slurs, intimidation, and the alleged use of forged signatures and documents to remove the Minister from her positions as a director in various companies.

The Special Investigation Team (SIT) has recorded the Minister’s statement and questioned her staff. Given the gravity of the matter, Dehradun SSP Pramendra Singh Dobal constituted an SIT—under the supervision of SP (Rural) Jaya Baluni—which has recorded the statement of Minister Rekha Arya. Additionally, members of the Minister’s staff have also been questioned.

title: Cyber fraud drains billions, but recovery is going low - The Rising Nepal
description: Cyber fraud drains billions, but recovery is going low  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter,Kathmandu, Nov. 3: The Nepal Police has received a positive response from the government to its proposal to establish an ‘Integrated Cyber Scam Response Centre,’ and preparations for setting up the specialised unit have begun.

With members of the public losing billions of rupees every year to cyber fraud, the police have been stressing the need for a dedicated specialised unit to tackle the growing menace.

As digital transactions involve banks and telecommunications service providers as well as other institutions, the police had submitted a proposal to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking an integrated and effective mechanism to respond to cyber scams, a senior police official told The Rising Nepal.

According to Deputy Inspector General and Spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle, the Ministry of Home Affairs has responded positively to the proposal. "Previously, the initiative could not move forward due to various constraints, including budgetary problems. This time, we have received a positive response from the ministry concerned, and I understand that correspondence has already been made with the relevant agencies," he said.

Security experts say that, alongside establishing such a centre, the government must also address procedural hurdles between agencies and increase the number and capacity of investigators.

"Such centres can particularly play a role in recovering money. Compared to investigations, there are more procedural complications involved in returning money lost to fraud," said former AIG Rajendra Singh Bhandari.

"These issues need to be addressed, while partnerships with other countries must also be strengthened to deal with cross-border money transfers," said Bhandari.

Only Rs. 180 M recovered out of 2B lost

A Kathmandu-based man, who lost Rs. 1.84 million in a cyber-scam last April and did not wish to disclose his identity, said he had managed to recover only Rs. 16,000 so far.

According to figures provided by Cyber Bureau officials, members of the public lost more than Rs. 2 billion to cyber fraud during the last fiscal year. However, only around Rs. 180 million of the amount was recovered. Of the 20,000 complaints related to cybercrime registered in the fiscal year 2082/83, B.S. around 7,500 were related to financial fraud.

According to DIG Kafle, an analysis of data from the past three years shows that only around eight per cent of the money lost to cyber fraud has been recovered. The police have attributed the low recovery rate to both legal and procedural complications.
